Conditions

1.   Pursuant to clause 27 of the Metropolitan Region Scheme, this approval is
     deemed to be an approval under clause 54(1) of the Metropolitan Region
     Scheme.

2.   This decision constitutes planning approval only and is valid for a period of four
     years from the date of approval. If the subject development is not substantially
     commenced within the specified period, the approval shall lapse and be of no
     further effect.

3.   Prior to applying for a Building Permit, the proponent shall submit to the City of
     Gosnells for approval a preliminary proposal for an art work designed by a
     professional artist at a cost of 1% of the total project cost (to a maximum of
     $250,000), to be located within the subject site as an integral part of the
     development. Alternatively, prior to occupation of the development, the
     owner/applicant shall make a cash contribution towards public art in lieu of the
     above.

     Prior to the commencement of development, and if not making a cash
     contribution, the proponent shall submit to the City of Gosnells for approval an
     'Application for Artwork Design' and the proponent is to enter into a contract with
     a professional artist/s to design and install (if appropriate) the artwork approved
     by the City of Gosnells.

     Prior to the occupation of the development, the art work shall then be installed
     and maintained thereafter to the satisfaction of the City of Gosnells.

     prepared and approved, in consultation with the Department of Water and
     Environmental Regulation, consistent with any approved Local Water
     Management Strategy.

     10), 329 (Lot 1) Kenwick Road and 582 (Lot 500) Bickley Road into one

Proposal:

The application proposes the construction of four warehouse buildings to
accommodate equipment for the purposes of data storage and includes provision for
a future electrical substation. The warehouses will be constructed in four separate
stages comprising:

•     Four, two storey buildings consisting of:
          o   Warehouse 1 – 9,429m² gross floor area (GFA)
          o   Warehouse 2 - 19,694m² GFA
          o   Warehouse 3 – 16,220m² GFA
          o   Warehouse 4 – 17,867m² GFA

•     A security gatehouse located adjacent to Kenwick Road.
•     Back up power generators.
•     Access from Bickley Road and Kenwick Road.
•     106 car parking bays.


                                                                           Page | 4
                                                                                       OFFICIAL




•   A maximum of 110 staff working from the site to maintain the data centre.


The construction of the associated electrical substation will be the subject of a future
development application.

Background:

The subject site is situated at the corner of Kelvin Road and Kenwick Road, with
access obtained via Kenwick Road and Bickley Road, and is currently vacant. The
proposal is within close proximity to, and abuts, the Tonkin Highway Primary Regional
Road Reserve. Kelvin Road is designated as an Other Regional Road under the
Metropolitan Region Scheme (MRS). A plan showing the location of the subject site
is contained in Attachment 1.

Planning Framework

The subject site forms part of the Maddington Kenwick Strategic Employment Area
(MKSEA), being land bound by Bickley Road, Tonkin Highway, the district boundary
with the City of Kalamunda and Roe Highway. The subject site is located within
Precinct 1 of the MKSEA, which comprises approximately 125ha of land bound by
Victoria Road, Tonkin Highway, Kelvin Road and Bickley Road in Maddington.

The City is currently progressing a Structure Plan (SP) for Precinct 1 (Attachment 3).
The draft SP is currently pending final determination by the Department of Planning
Lands and Heritage (DPLH). As the draft SP has been advertised and endorsed
by Council, it is a seriously entertained planning document.

Legislation and Policy:

Legislation

•      Planning and Development Act 2005
•      Planning and Development (Local Planning Schemes) Regulations 2015.
•      Metropolitan Region Scheme
•      Town Planning Scheme No. 6

Local Policies

Local Planning Policy 5.6 – Maddington Kenwick Strategic Employment Area

The proposal was not required to be advertised for public comment.

Planning Assessment:

Town Planning Scheme No. 6

Land Use Permissibility

Table 1 of TPS 6 (Zoning Table) does not specify land use permissibility for the
Business Development zone. Rather it states that development and use of land is to
be in accordance with an adopted structure plan (SP). Whilst there is no approved SP,
the draft MKSEA Precint 1 Structure Plan identifies the subject land for General
Industry. Under TPS 6, a Warehouse is a ‘D’ use in the General Industry zone,
meaning that the use is not permitted unless the local government has exercised its
discretion by granting planning approval. The proposal is therefore capable of approval
under the planning framework.

Car Parking

The following table details TPS 6 parking provisions for the site.

    Use Class    TPS      6    Parking    TPS 6 Car Parking Car       Parking
                 Standards                Requirements          Bays Provided
    Warehouse    1 space for every        Warehouse 1: 9,429m²
                 100m² gross floor        Warehouse 2: 19,694m²
                 area, plus               Warehouse 3: 16,220m²
                                          Warehouse 4: 17,868m²

The proposal results in a significant shortfall of 638 parking bays when assessed
against the parking requirements of TPS 6. In this regard however, the proposal is not
representative of a typical warehouse development as it involves the storage of self-
sustaining computer servers which requires significantly less staff and/or visitors to the
site. If the car parking is assessed against the proposed number of employees, the car
parking shortfall would be four car parking bays.

The applicant submitted a Traffic Impact Assessment (TIA) which provided parking
demand modelling to estimate the parking demand for the site, based on the estimated

                                                                                Page | 6
                                                                                            OFFICIAL




number of staff. The TIA indicates 80% of staff are likely drive a car to the site daily. In
addition to this, the development provides end of trip facilities to encourage staff to use
alternative forms of transport. The TIA suggests a peak parking demand of 88 bays for
the development.

Clause 4.13.3 of TPS 6 allows for variations to car parking requirements where there
will be no resultant lowering of safety, convenience, or amenity standards. Based on
the use of the site it is considered that that there will be no resultant lowering of safety,
convenience, and amenity standards resulting from the proposed variation and
therefore the proposed parking is considered appropriate and acceptable.

Setbacks and Landscaping

The proposal complies with the setback and landscaping requirements of TPS 6, with
the exception of the following:

  Assessment
                   TPS 6 Standards                                Assessment
    Element

In considering the setback variations, it is noted that the proposed building setback is
unlikely to have a negative impact on the amenity of the locality and any impact is
proposed to be minimised using landscaping within the site and on the adjacent verge.
The variation is considered minor and as such, the proposed setback is considered
acceptable.

In considering the landscaping variation, the reduced landscaping strip directly adjoins
a large verge area to be landscaped which will lessen the impact of the reduction. It
should also be noted that there is additional landscaping provided within the site which
will contribute to the amenity of the area. As such, the proposed reduction in
landscaping abutting Kenwick Road is considered acceptable.

Local Planning Policy 5.6 - MKSEA Precinct 1

Local Planning Policy 5.6 - Maddington Kenwick Strategic Employment Area (LPP 5.6)
provides guidance for the assessment and determination of applications for
subdivision and development approval for land within the MKSEA in the absence of an
adopted Structure Plan. In this regard, Clause 4.3 of LPP 5.6 states:

        "Council will generally not support applications for development of land unless,
        in Council’s opinion, approval and implementation of the proposal will not:



                                                                                   Page | 7
                                                                                        OFFICIAL




       (a)     Compromise the value or wellbeing of any environmental feature.

       (b)     Have an unreasonable impact on nearby residential and/or rural zoned
               properties. Such impacts include, but are not limited to, noise, dust,
               odour, vibration and traffic."

In considering the application, the following is relevant:

•      The proposed development does not affect any land that is of environmental
       significance.
•      The proposed development doesn’t have an unreasonable impact on adjoining
       properties which are zoned for industrial purposes.

In the case of the MKSEA Precinct 1 Structure Plan, planning is well advanced and is
expected to be finalised imminently. The proposal is not considered to jeopardise the
structure plan or ongoing development of the MKSEA Precinct 1 area.

Traffic and Access

The application proposes access to the site via a single crossover to Kenwick Road,
with egress from Bickley Road via two crossovers, including an emergency crossover.

The proposal was referred to MRWA due to the site abutting a portion of Tonkin
Highway Road Reserve. MRWA supports the development, subject to the inclusion of
relevant conditions and advice notes which, should DAP approve the proposal, should
be imposed.

The applicant submitted a Traffic Impact Assessment (TIA) (Attachment 5) to support
the application which indicates that traffic generated from the development will not
have an adverse impact on the surrounding road network, and there is sufficient
capacity within the network to accommodate the development. The recommendations
of the TIA are:

•   The Kenwick Road pavement and seal be widened to support two-way traffic
    movements up to the substation access crossover.
•   The intersection of Kenwick Road / Kelvin Road should be configured as left-in/left-
    out (right turn movements to be banned). Banning the right turn out movements
    will need to be enforced through intersection modifications including islands,
    signage and line marking.

With regard to the above, should DAP approve the proposal, a condition should be
imposed requiring the applicant to implement the recommendations of the TIA.

It should be noted that the MKSEA Precinct 1 Structure Plan contemplates the
extension of Kenwick Road through to Bickley Road to support the future development
of the area. The extension of this road was intended to provide a road frontage to
enable the future subdivision and development of the adjoining properties. As the
proposed development will be undertaken over a large portion of the developable area
within this precinct, the requirement for the extension of Kenwick Road is no longer
required. In this regard, the development of the remaining lots within this precinct will
be able to obtain direct vehicle access from Bickley Road. The City has considered the


                                                                               Page | 8
                                                                                        OFFICIAL




requirement for the extension of Kenwick Road and support the removal of the road in
this location.

Bushfire Planning

The site is located within a Bushfire Prone Area and was referred to DFES. DFES has
no objection to the proposal and provided advice regarding the vegetation assessment
for the Tonkin Highway reserve. DFES has questioned the vegetation assessment
within the Tonkin Highway reserve and noted that the vegetation classification will
affect the subsequent BAL rating for the proposed substation site, however, would not
impact the BAL ratings applicable to the warehouse buildings. In this regard DFES
recommend the BMP be updated to accurately assess the vegetation within the Tonkin
Highway reserve. As development of the substation site is not included in this
application, a condition requiring amendments to the BMP is not necessary. However,
should DAP approve the proposal, an advice note should be imposed advising the
applicant of the DFES requirements to reassess the vegetation classification within the
Tonkin Highway reserve as part of the future development application for the
substation site.

Dampier to Bunbury Pipeline

The City consulted with DPLH due to the site being located within the Dampier to
Bunbury Natural Gas Pipeline (DBNGP) corridor. DPLH advised that the proposed
development is not expected to materially interfere with the exercise of rights that have
been, or might in the future be, conferred under section 34 of the Dampier to Bunbury
Pipeline Act 1997 (DBP Act). Further, the Dampier Bunbury Pipeline (DBP) as owners
and operators of the Dampier to Bunbury Natural Gas Pipeline (DBNGP) advised the
City that they have no objection to the development application.

Conclusion:

The proposal is consistent with the planning framework and is therefore recommended
for approval subject to conditions.

                 1.0 Introduction
                 Developed on behalf of the landowners and for No. 307, 323, 329 Kenwick Road, Maddington
                 and 582 Bickley Road, Maddington for a proposed industrial development across four separate
                 lots, comprising of four (4), two-storey Data Centres (Warehouse) inclusive of multiple associated
                 power generators and front of house offices, each with an independent staff and guest car park.


                 The development site is located within a Business Development Zone of the City of Gosnells Local
                 Planning Scheme No. 6 area, within an industrial development area of the suburb of Maddington,
                 abutting Tonkin Highway. The development proposal is consistent with the planning objectives
                 for the locality as it is conducive with the current nature of established land uses. Despite being
                 in a zone that requires a Local Structure Plan, the absence of one does not preclude support of
                 the intended planning outcome.


                 Preliminary design review has been sought through a City of Gosnells Pre-Lodgement meeting
                 on the 12th of March 2024, with the initial feedback and correspondence between the City, the
                 landowners (Canberra Data Centres Pty Ltd) and the proponent (Developed) forming the basis of
                 the development proposal. It is the strong preference of Canberra Data Centres to engage the
                 determining authority prior to the submission of a Development Assessment Panel (DAP)
                 application to gauge and understand the planning complexities development area and locally
                 driven priorities of the City of Gosnells.


                 During the initial stages of the design review process, the City advised that there was not
                 requirement to attend the Design Review Panel (DRP), as the industrial natural of the proposal
                 did not trigger a detailed design review.


                 In the absence of requiring a design review, the Architect EJE has prepared a high-level review of
                 State Planning Policy 7.0’s assessment of the 10 design principles to further bolster the
                 development as a positive design outcome for the Maddington locality. In addition, the design
                 team comprises of expert technicians which have been engaged to provide planning, design,
                 landscape and operational advice for transport, waste and sustainability measures.


                 This report intends to provide a comprehensive planning assessment against the State and Local
                 government planning framework, and details performance against the applicable objectives and
                 requirements. This in part will demonstrate that the proposal is of an appropriate built form, a
                 quality design, resulting in an overall development proposal that is appropriate for development
                 approval.

                 2.0 Development Background
                 2.1       Site Context

                 The subject development site is allocated amongst four large lots located at No. 307, 323, 329
                 Kenwick Road and 582 Bickley Road. Each lot has multiple frontages due to the size of the lots
                 spanding an average frontage of 100 metres to each respective lot boundary. The four Lots equal
                 76,037m2. The lots are located within the suburb of Maddington and situated within an Industrial
                 area. As indicated by the Regional and Local Context Map, the site is framed by Tonkin Highway
                 to the east, Kelvin Road to the northwest, Kenwick Road which could be considered as a minor
                 road located to the north and Bickley Road located to the south.


                 Development           within   the      immediate     locality   has     historically   been   large-scale
                 industrial/commercial development. It is unlikely that the locality will transition into any land use
                 other than industrial and commercial. The subject site is located approximately 15km to Perth
                 Central Business District, 10km from Perth International Airport and 25km to Fremantle. Although
                 situated in the east of Perth, the site is well positioned to most notable infrastructure and
                 transport nodes.


                 The most notable landmark is the Boral Quarries located approximately 1.7km southeast. The
                 Quarries have consistently provided business to the Maddington industrial area. Other notable
                 landmarks are Orange Grove Primary School approximately 350m past Tonkin Highway to the
                 east and a series of High Frequency Bus routes 229/279 (<50m walkable catchment zone).

                 2.2       Development Proposal

                 The proposed development comprises of four (4) warehouse buildings each building paired with
                 multiple generators for each respective warehouse and outdoor vehicle parking. Each
                 Warehouse, known as a data centre for the purposes of the application, are large structures,
                 inclusive of predominantly self-sufficient machinery and minimal service personnel operators,
                 with the exception of a handful of transient personnel, the data centre’s function and operate
                 independently.


                 Access into the site is self-contained due to the limited traffic movement necessary for the data
                 centres. Primary access is proposed via Kenwick Road (north-east). Once entered the site via the
                 entry gatehouse, traffic is directed to exit via Brickley Road. The consolidated traffic movement
                 enables smooth ingress and egress to and from the site.


                 Due to the self-contained, independent nature of the Data Centres, there is no expectation for a
                 significant number of patrons to occupy the facility. Therefore, parking has been reduced to a
                 total of 110 bays, inclusive of disability parking and EV charging bays.

                 3.0 Planning Framework & Assessment
                 3.1       Strategic Planning Framework - Perth and Peel @ 3.5million

                 Perth and Peel@3.5million is the overarching strategic planning framework for the Perth and Peel
                 metropolitan regions. Perth and Peel@3.5million proposes five strategic themes for a liveable,
                 prosperous, connected, sustainable and collaborative city. The framework aspires to a city that
                 provides a network of connected activity centres which deliver employment, entertainment and
                 high-density lifestyle choices.


                 South Metropolitan Peel sub-region will experience strong growth, with the population expected
                 to more than double from 523,400 people in 2011 to 1.26 million by 2050. The south-east sector
                 had an estimated population of 10.7% of the total regional population. More than half of all
                 residents lived within the City of Gosnells. Therefore, industrial centres within the City are needed
                 as they are generally associated with employment infrastructure, assisting the economic growth
                 within the sector. The proposed Data Centre (warehouse) will help the City meet its strategic
                 targets set by the State government.

                 3.2       City of Gosnells Local Planning Strategy

                 The Local Planning Strategy is the key strategic planning document for the City of Gosnells. While
                 much of the City is developed for single residential housing, significant areas of infill development
                 have occurred in the older suburbs of Beckenham, Kenwick, Maddington and Gosnells. The City
                 also encompasses large areas of rural zoned land in the Darling Range and foothills, district open
                 space and industrial areas.


                 The major employment area in the City is the Maddington Industrial area which is the largest
                 industrial area in the City was established in the 1970s. This industrial area is now fully developed
                 with only a few vacant lots remaining. The City has a strong proclivity towards employment
                 opportunities within these industrial areas due to the expansive nature of labour orientated
                 development. The Maddington Industrial area is the ideal location for the proposed data centres
                 as it will seamlessly integrate into the existing built form and provide the targeted employment.

                 3.3       Planning & Development Act 2005 – Metropolitan Region Scheme

                 The subject site is zoned ‘Industrial’ under the Metropolitan Region Scheme (MRS). The Industrial
                 zone is defined as – to provide for manufacturing industry, the storage and distribution of goods
                 and associated uses. The aims of MRS industrial zone are met through the proposed development,
                 delivering a land use of strategic importance and where possible preventing use conflicts and
                 environmental impacts.


                 3.4       City of Gosnells Local Planning Scheme No. 6

                 In accordance with the City of Gosnells Local Planning Scheme No. 6 (LPS 6), the subject site is
                 zoned ‘Business Development’. The zone enables the creation of a local structure plan.


                 In the context of the Scheme, there is no applicable local structure plan that directly relates to
                 the development, despite what is contained in a Local Planning Policy 5.6 – Maddington Kenwick
                 Employment Area (LPP5.6 MKSEA) which is understood to be the prevailing framework in lieu of
                 a structure plan. Therefore, in the absence of a structure plan, the Scheme’s planning controls
                 shall prevail.


                 The Maddington Kenwick Strategic Employment Area Precinct 3A does not apply as the
                 development site sits outside of the redevelopment area.

                 3.6       Local Planning Policy 5.6 - Maddington Kenwick Strategic Employment
                           Area (MKSEA)

                 The City of Gosnells Local Planning Policy 5.6 was prepared to provide guidance for subdivision
                 and development within the identified Maddington Kenwick Strategic Employment Area, known
                 as MKSEA. This area was historically reserved for rural developments, however, recent changes to
                 the City’s local framework, have identified there is an economic preference for industrial areas.


                 The WAPC has formally advised the City of Gosnells that Structure Plans are required for all land
                 within the MKSEA, so as to guide subdivision and development in that area.


                 With regards to the proposed development and the absence of a Structure Plan, the City is able
                 to consider development proposals in the absence of a required Structure Plan and there may be
                 situations where it is appropriate to support such proposals, so long as they do not prejudice the
                 delivery of long-term plans for the area.


                 The development is understood to be in the MKSEA Precinct 1 and is bound by Bickley Road,
                 Victoria Road and Tonkin Highway. Planning is underway to develop the land into a major
                 industrial area. As of December 2022, it is understood that the Structure Plan for Precinct 1 is still
                 being modified to update supporting technical documents and seek endorsement from servicing
                 authorities and state government agencies.

                 5.0 Design Performance
                 5.1       SPP 7.0 – Design Principles Assessment

                 The development application plans and supporting documentation have been designed and
                 prepared in accordance with the ten principles of good design as set out in State Planning Policy
                 7.0 Design of the Built Environment. A summary of the development application against the ten
                 principles has been prepared by EJE Architects as provided below.

                     Principle 1              The proposed development takes contextual cues from nearby
                     Context and              industrial development of similar scale buildings. This relevant context
                     Character                includes industrial development to the west of the site along Bickley
                                              Road, and larger scale industrial development in Kenwick Road.


                                              The design response starts from these contextual inputs but is elevated
                                              to reflect the capital investment of the development. The contextual
                                              industrial typology involving large format warehouse or workshop
                                              spaces with attached more refined articulated administrative/office
                                              workspace positioned at the public interface of the site, is maintained
                                              and reinforced with the proposed design of the development.


                     Principle 2              The landscape design by Terras Landscape Architects incorporates
                     Landscape Quality        ornamental planting in prominent locations, particularly around the
                                              main site entrance and building frontages, to enhance visual appeal and
                                              create a welcoming environment.


                                              An irrigation system is proposed to support the successful
                                              establishment and long-term health of the planting scheme. Due to
                                              significant underground services, there are notable constraints on
                                              where canopy trees can be planted. In response, canopy tree planting
                                              has been strategically optimised within available areas, utilising a
                                              combination of native species and ornamental feature trees at key entry
                                              points to provide structure and seasonal interest. The understorey
                                              planting has been carefully selected to ensure low maintenance
                                              requirements while maintaining strong visual amenity and ecological
                                              resilience. These selections aim to deliver a robust, enduring landscape
                                              that complements the site’s functional needs.


                     Principle 3              The    proposed    development     includes     multiple   buildings   of
                     Built form & scale       predominantly two-storey form, capped by low pitch roofs to minimise
                                              the building volume beyond the minimum heights operationally
                                              required to accommodate functional equipment and internal building
                                              services. The enclosed building volumes are capped by roof level plant
                                              decks, located to provide efficient building services routes and
                                              reticulation.

                     Sustainability    which is a closed-loop chilled water-cooling system, which results in

                 5.2       Local Planning Scheme ‘Deemed Provisions’ Clause 67

                 In considering an application for development approval the decision maker is to have due regard
                 to the matters outlined in clause 67(2) of the deemed provisions to the extent that, in the opinion

                 This development application seeks approval for a proposed industrial development, for a Data

                 Maddington.


                 The development application is highly consistent with the objectives and planning intent of the
                 state and local government statutory planning framework that applies to the subject site and the
                 proposed land use.


                 The proposed development has been planned and designed with close consideration for the
                 requirements and intended outcomes of the objectives of the Business Development Zone and
                 the City of Gosnells Local Planning Scheme No. 6, and in anticipation for the Draft Local Planning
                 Scheme No. 24. The development is consistent with the sustainable industrial development and
                 aims for the Scheme. The proposed development will provide increased workplaces and land
                 use diversity within the area.


                 In anticipation of a packaged DAP report, we humbly request the City of Gosnells consider the
                 application for acceptance so that the full application package can be supplied for the City’s
                 ultimate assessment and recommendation for endorsement.

         1 Executive summary

         This Transport Impact Assessment (TIA) has been prepared by Urbii on behalf of CDC Data
         Centres Pty Ltd for the proposed development of a data centre at 307–329 Kenwick Road,
         Maddington. The subject site is located within the Maddington Kenwick Strategic Employment
         Area (MKSEA) and includes four data centre buildings with a total gross floor area of
         approximately 64,000 square metres. The development will accommodate up to 110 staff and
         will be supported by a substation, security gatehouse, internal circulation roads, and end-of-trip
         facilities including showers, change rooms and lockers. Vehicle access to the site will be via a
         full movement crossover on Kenwick Road, with secondary exit-only and emergency access
         provided on Bickley Road.
         A total of 106 car parking bays will be provided, including six ACROD bays and ten bays with
         electric vehicle charging infrastructure. In addition, 28 bicycle parking spaces will be distributed
         across the site to support sustainable transport options. Based on staff projections and mode
         share assumptions, the peak parking demand is estimated at 88 bays, indicating that the
         proposed supply is sufficient to accommodate both staff and visitors.
         The proposed development is expected to generate approximately 685 vehicle trips per day,
         including 104 trips in the morning peak hour and 90 trips in the afternoon peak hour. The traffic
         impact has been assessed using SIDRA modelling software for 2027 and 2037 planning
         horizons. All modelled intersections, including the key intersections of Kelvin Road with Kenwick
         Road and Bickley Road, are forecast to operate at Level of Service A, with minimal delays and
         acceptable queue lengths under both existing and future traffic scenarios.
         As part of the development, the intersection of Kenwick Road and Kelvin Road will be
         reconfigured to a left-in / left-out only arrangement, with all right-turn movements prohibited. This
         change is required by Main Roads WA to accommodate future Restricted Access Vehicle (RAV
         7) movements and to align with the broader objectives of the Tonkin Highway Corridor Upgrade.
         The modifications will be implemented through median extensions, physical islands, signage
         and line marking. In addition, the section of Kenwick Road leading to the development access
         will be widened to support two-way vehicle movement.
         The traffic analysis confirms that the proposed development can be accommodated by the
         existing transport network, with minimal impact on surrounding intersections and road safety.
         Overall, the development integrates well with the existing and planned transport infrastructure
         and is considered appropriate from a traffic and transport perspective.

         2 Introduction

         This Transport Impact Assessment has been prepared by Urbii on behalf of CDC
         Data Centres Pty Ltd with regards to the proposed data centre development,
         located at 307-329 Kenwick Rd, Maddington.
         The subject site is situated on the southern side of Kenwick Road, as shown in Figure 1. A
         portion of the site extends to Bickley Road. It is proposed to develop the site into a data centre.
         The aim of this Transport Impact Assessment (TIA) is to assess the impact of the proposal on
         the existing transport network. The TIA was prepared in accordance with the WAPC Transport
         Assessment Guidelines 2016.

         3.1 Existing site use, access and parking
         The subject site is mostly vacant. The north-west portion of the site is used as a heavy vehicle

         3.2 Surrounding road network and traffic management on roads
         Information from online mapping services, Main Roads WA, Local Government,
         and site visits was collected to assess the existing traffic management on frontage
         roads.


         3.2.1 Kelvin Road
         Kelvin Road near the subject site is an approximately 22m wide, four-lane dual carriageway
         road. It features a wide, kerbed and landscaped median with tree planting. A path for walking
         and cycling is provided on the northern side of the road. It is classified as a Distributor A road in
         the Main Roads WA road hierarchy (Figure 4) and operates under a posted speed limit of 70km/h
         (Figure 5).
         Distributor A roads are the responsibility of Local Government and are typically for high capacity
         traffic movements between industrial, commercial and residential areas. (Figure 6).


         3.2.2 Kenwick Road
         Kenwick Road is approximately 360m in length, forming a T-intersection with Kelvin Road to the
         west and ending in a culdesac to the east. The width of the road seal varies from 9.5m width up
         to the existing site crossover, to 4.5m width at the eastern end of the road.
         No footpath is provided.
         Kenwick Road is classified as an Access road in the Main Roads WA road hierarchy (Figure 4)
         and operates under the default speed limit of 50km/h (Figure 5). Access roads are normally the
         responsibility of Local Government. They are predominantly for the provision of vehicle access
         to abutting properties. (Figure 6).
         It is recommended that the Kenwick Road pavement and seal be widened to support two-
         way traffic movements, up to the development access crossover.


         3.2.3 Bickley Road
         Bickley Road is approximately 780m in length, forming a 4-way roundabout intersection with
         Kelvin Road to the west and terminating at the Tonkin Highway road reservation to the east. The
         road has a 9.5m wide seal and no footpaths are provided.
         Bickley Road is classified as an Access road in the Main Roads WA road hierarchy (Figure 4)
         and operates under the default speed limit of 50km/h (Figure 5). Access roads are normally the
         responsibility of Local Government. They are predominantly for the provision of vehicle access
         to abutting properties. (Figure 6).

         3.8 Bicycle access
         The Perth and Peel Long Term Cycle Network (LTCN) designates routes by their function, rather
         than built form. Function considers the type of activities that take place along a route, and the
         level of demand (existing and potential). The built form of a route is based on the characteristics
         of the environment, including space availability, topography, traffic conditions (speed, volumes),
         and primary users. The cycling network hierarchy is described in Figure 13.

         3.9 Crash data and safety
         The five-year crash history in the vicinity of the site was obtained from Main Roads WA. As
         detailed in Table 2, 29 crashes were recorded in the locality. This includes 23 crashes recorded
         at the roundabout intersection of Kelvin Road and Bickley Road. The crash map is presented in
         Figure 16.
         Most crashes were property damage only in severity, with four medical severity crashes. The
         crash data is summarised in Table 2.
         The proposed development will result in a less than 3% increase in traffic at the roundabout
         intersection. This is within the typical variation of day-to-day traffic at the intersection, which will
         not be noticeable. The low proportion of traffic generated by the development is unlikely to impact
         road safety at the roundabout.

         4 Development proposal

         The proposal for the subject site is for a data centre development, comprising:
             •   Four data centre buildings, delivering a total of around 64,000m2 GFA;
             •   A substation and generators to power the data centre;
             •   A security gatehouse at the main site entry;
             •   An internal circulation road network with integrated pedestrian crossings;
             •   106 car parking bays distributed throughout the site;
             •   3 x loading docks;
             •   28 bicycle parking spaces; and,

         servicing will be accommodated within the loading docks distributed throughout the site.
         People walking and cycling will access the development from the external road network adjacent
         to the site. Bicycle parking is distributed throughout the site.

         Crossover sightline assessment


         The crossover sight distance assessment was undertaken in accordance with the Austroads
         Guide to Road Design Part 3 – Geometric Design (AGRD03).
         Stopping Sight Distance (SSD) is the distance to enable a normally alert driver, travelling at
         the design speed on wet pavement, to perceive, react and brake to a stop before reaching a
         hazard on the road ahead.
         SSD is derived from two components:
         1. The distance travelled during the total reaction time
         2. The distance travelled during the braking time from the design speed to a stop and their
         relationship is shown in Equation 1.




         A reaction time of 2.5 seconds was adopted for the analysis, which is conservative as it assumes
         the driver is not alert. An operating speed of 50km/h was adopted. The coefficient of deceleration
         is 0.36. The calculated Stopping Sight Distance (SSD) is detailed in Table 3.
         The required Stopping Sight Distance is 62m. The sight distance sketch in Appendix E
         confirms sufficient sightlines are available for the development crossovers.


         Table 3: Stopping Sight Distance calculation

           Parameter                   Value   Units
           Rt                          2.5     sec

           V                           50      km/h

           d                           0.36

           a                           0%

           SSD required                62      m

         Information from relevant planning documents, Main Roads WA, Department of

         6.1 Tonkin Highway Corridor (MRWA)
         Main Roads WA is undertaking the Tonkin Highway Corridor project, from Roe Highway to Kelvin
         Road (Figure 19).
         The project will upgrade Tonkin Highway from Roe Highway to Kelvin Road, to improve safety
         and reduce delays along the heavily congested route.
         The scope of works include:
             • Widening Tonkin Highway from four to six lanes from south of Roe Highway to Kelvin Road
             • Grade separations (Tonkin Highway travelling over intersections at):
               − Tonkin Highway / Welshpool Road – Connections to and from Tonkin Highway north and
                  south
               − Tonkin Highway / Hale Road – Partial connection with north-facing ramps (to and from
                  the airport and Perth)
               − Tonkin Highway / Kelvin Road – Connections to and from Tonkin Highway north and
                  south
             • Median and verge barriers
             • Principal Shared Path connecting to existing paths north on Tonkin Highway, including
               underpasses at ramps at the new intersections
             • Lighting and noise walls
             • Local urban design and landscaping opportunities.

         6.2 Intersection of Kelvin Rd / Kenwick Rd
         As part of a proposed data centre and warehouse development in Maddington, the intersection
         of Kelvin Road and Kenwick Road is subject to reconfiguration to support evolving traffic
         demands and regional planning objectives.
         The Transport Impact Assessment (TIA) submitted for the development initially proposed a left-
         in/right-in/left-out configuration for this intersection, with right-turn-out movements prohibited.
         However, Main Roads WA (MRWA) has advised that this arrangement is not consistent with
         their future design for the area.
         MRWA requires the intersection to be reconfigured to left-in/left-out only, thereby eliminating all
         right-turn movements. This revision has been reflected in the amended TIA, along with updated
         traffic distribution and associated impact assessments.
         The rationale behind this restriction is primarily to support RAV 7 vehicle movements and broader
         freight efficiency objectives identified in the MKSEA (Maddington Kenwick Strategic Employment
         Area) Master Plan.

         8 Traffic assessment

         8.1 Assessment period
         Two time periods are considered in the traffic assessment:
             • Weekday AM peak hour: 7:00am to 8:00am.
             • Weekday PM peak hour: 3:00pm to 4:00pm.

         The analysis was undertaken for the following scenarios:
             •   Existing situation (without proposed development traffic).
             •   2027 (without development traffic).
             •   2027 (with development traffic included).
             •   2037 (without development traffic).
             •   2037 (with development traffic included).

         When the existing situation was modelled, the SIDRA intersection performance results
         indicated there is currently limited capacity for right turn movements from Kenwick Road
         to Kelvin Road.
         Therefore, the intersection of Kenwick Road / Kelvin Road will need to be reconfigured as left-
         in/left-out to support the proposed development.
         Banning the right turn movements will need to be enforced through intersection modifications
         including filling of the right turn pocket, extension of the Kelvin Road median across the
         intersection, signage and line marking, which are recommended to be completed as part of the
         proposed development.




         8.2 Existing traffic flows
         To establish existing base traffic flows on the surrounding road network and nearby intersections,
         Urbii undertook a survey of turning movements and queuing at the intersection of Kelvin Road
         and Kenwick Road. Main Roads WA data was obtained for the roundabout intersection of Kelvin
         Road / Bickley Road, which was factored up to match the existing assessment year.
         The traffic count survey was undertaken on a standard weekday in February 2025 between
         7:00am to 8:00am and 3:00pm to 4:00pm.
         The base peak hour traffic flows derived for analysis are detailed in Appendix B.

         8.5 10-year post development forecasting
         Forecasting background traffic volumes for the 10 year post development scenario is a complex
         exercise. Transport demand forecasting is shifting from fixed forecasts to ‘scenario modelling.’
         Scenario modelling recognises that there are multiple known and unknown disrupters to
         transport behaviour in the coming years, for example:
             •   Increased work from home activity;
             •   Increased popularity of micromobility devices such as e-scooters;
             •   Increased provision of public transport such as light rail and trackless trams;
             •   Electric Vehicles;
             •   Autonomous Vehicles; and,
             •   Government Net Zero emission targets.

         This TIA adopts a conservative compounded annual growth rate of 2.02%, which is similar to
         traffic growth on Tonkin Highway near the site, from 2020 to 2025.

         Reference was made to Austroads guidelines to help identify which modelled intersections
         should be further assessed in SIDRA. The traffic volume thresholds adopted for further analysis
         are set out in Figure 20. The development crossovers are expected to function at a satisfactory
         level of service A. No SIDRA analysis is required for the crossovers, as peak hour traffic volumes
         fall below the thresholds in Figure 20.




         Figure 20: Austroads guidance on the assessment of intersections


         Capacity analysis of the intersection of Kelvin Road / Kenwick Road and Kelvin Road / Bickley
         Road was undertaken using the SIDRA 9 computer software package. SIDRA 9 is an
         intersection modelling tool commonly used by traffic engineers for all types of intersections.
         The SIDRA model for the existing Kelvin Road / Kenwick Road intersection is presented in Figure
         21. When the existing situation was modelled, the SIDRA intersection performance results
         indicated there is currently limited capacity for right turn movements from Kenwick Road to Kelvin
         Road.
         It should be noted that the right turn capacity constraint is an existing issue. However, the existing
         traffic volumes are low, so the intersection is currently functional. To support increased traffic
         from the proposed development, the right turn movements at the intersection should be banned.
         The 2027 and 2037 network assumes that the intersection of Kenwick Road / Kelvin Road will
         be configured as left-in/left-out (Figure 22).
         A summary of the analysis results is presented in Table 6.


         Overall, the SIDRA results indicate that the proposed development will have a minimal
         impact on the road network.


         The intersection and development crossovers operate at a good level of service with minimal
         queueing and delays.
         Detailed SIDRA outputs for each intersection are provided in Appendix C.

         8.7 Impact on neighbouring areas
         The traffic generated by the proposed development is not expected to significantly affect
         surrounding areas and the proposed land uses are in line with planning for the local area.
         Therefore, there is not expected to be any impact on neighbouring areas that would require any
         further consideration.


         8.8 Traffic noise and vibration
         It requires a doubling of traffic volumes on a road to produce a perceptible 3dB (A) increase in
         road noise. The proposed development will not increase traffic volumes or noise on surrounding
         roads anywhere near this level to result in any perceptible increase in noise.

         9.2 Parking requirements
         Advice provided by the project Town Planner indicates that the applicable planning scheme will
         result in a significant ‘on-paper’ parking shortfall.


         9.3 Parking demand modelling
         Urbii has undertaken an independent parking demand modelling exercise, to estimate the
         parking demand for the site, based on the number of staff anticipated to work at the data centre.
         As detailed in Figure 24, census data indicates that around 73% of workers in the City of Gosnells
         travelled to work by driving a car.
         An 80% car driver mode share is considered a reasonable target for staff working at the data
         centre, which is located within short walking distance of bus stops.
         The proposed development provides end of trip facilities including a shower, changing room and
         lockers plus bicycle parking for staff, to further encourage sustainable transport to the site.
         This results in an anticipated peak parking demand of 88 bays for 110 staff.
         The proposed development car parking provision is expected to be satisfactory for the needs of
         the data centre. There is sufficient car parking for staff and visitors.

         14 Conclusion

         This Transport Impact Assessment has been prepared by Urbii on behalf of CDC
         Data Centres Pty Ltd with regards to the proposed data centre development,
         located at 307-329 Kenwick Rd, Maddington.
         The subject site is situated on the southern side of Kenwick Road. A portion of the site extends
         to Bickley Road. It is proposed to develop the site into a data centre with up to 110 staff.
         The site promotes good connectivity with the existing road, public transport, and cycling network.
         The traffic analysis undertaken in this report shows that the traffic generation of the proposed
         development can be accommodated by the surrounding roads and intersections.
         The car parking supply is satisfactory and can accommodate the car parking demand of the
         proposed development.
         The following recommendations are made for subsequent stages of the proposed development:
             • The Kenwick Road pavement and seal be widened to support two-way traffic movements
               up to the substation access crossover.
             • The intersection of Kenwick Road / Kelvin Road should be configured as left-in/left-out
               (right turn movements to be banned). Banning the right turn out movements will need to be
               enforced through intersection modifications including islands, signage and line marking,
               which are recommended to be completed as part of the proposed development.

         It is concluded that the findings of this Transport Impact Assessment are supportive of the
         proposed development.

         Appendix C: SIDRA analysis outputs

         SIDRA outputs are presented in the form of Degree of Saturation, Level of Service,
         Average Delay and 95% Queue. These characteristics are defined as follows:


             • Degree of Saturation (DoS): is the ratio of the arrival traffic flow to the capacity of the
               approach during the same period. The Degree of Saturation ranges from close to zero for
               varied traffic flow up to one for saturated flow or capacity.
             • Level of Service (LoS): is the qualitative measure describing operational conditions
               within a traffic stream and the perception by motorists and/or passengers. In general, there
               are 6 levels of service, designated from A to F, with Level of Service A representing the
               best operating condition (i.e. free flow) and Level of Service F the worst (i.e. forced or
               breakdown flow).
             • Average Delay: is the average of all travel time delays for vehicles through the
               intersection.
             • 95% Queue: is the queue length below which 95% of all observed queue lengths fall.

            Executive Summary
            Stantec has been appointed by CDC Data Centres, c/o Developed Property to undertake an acoustic
            assessment for the proposed new 145MW data centre facility at 582 Bickley Rd, Maddington WA 6109. The
            proposed development includes four (4) two storey data centre buildings.
            To support the Development Application for the project, a noise impact assessment has been carried out, with
            predicted emissions assessed against the WA Environmental Protection (Noise) Regulations 1997 (EPNR).
            A 3D noise model was developed using the software package SoundPLAN v9.0, with noise emissions assessed
            for the worst-case operations.
            Results from the assessment show that with appropriate equipment selections and acoustic mitigation
            strategies, the site is expected to comply with the applicable EPNR noise emission criteria.
            Mechanical Plant and Back-up Generators
            The following acoustic mitigation measures are expected to be required to achieve the applicable limits under
            typical weather conditions:
                    Enclosed generator sets with acoustic attenuation applied to intake, discharge and exhaust. Preliminary
                    attenuation insertion loss values are provided in Appendix C;
                    Back-up Generators are to be tested 1 unit at a time, during daytime hours (Monday to Friday 0900-
                    1600hr). During an emergency (power outage) with up to 35 generators operating, exceedance of the
                    EPNR criteria may occur at night-time, however based on grid availability statistics from Western Power,
                    outages are likely to occur less than 0.07% of the year;

                    Design and selection of air-cooled Chillers and Package Units (PAC) to achieve acoustic emission
                    performance no higher than that detailed in Appendix C;
                    Design of Chillers and PAC units to achieve 75% speed during evening periods and 50% speed during
                    night-time periods (as defined in the EPNR);
                    Limiting the number of Chillers and PAC units operating based on time of the day (periods as defined in
                    the EPNR), as detailed in Section 4.3;
                    During the most sensitive periods; Sundays, Evenings and Night-times (as defined in the EPNR), the
                    selection of Chiller units operating will need to be managed such that the operational units are positioned
                    towards the middle of the buildings, away from sensitive receivers;
                    Under worst-case weather conditions, including thermal inversions, a marginal exceedance of +1 dB may
                    be expected at some receivers. This is considered not to be a perceptible difference.
            Waste Collection and Loading Dock
            It is noted that loading docks are located adjacent to the data centre building. Vehicles of various sizes up to
            19m semi-articulated trucks will be servicing the proposed development. Based on the existing adjacent uses
            (truck and industrial vehicle storage yards), the noise emission from trucks accessing the site are not expected
            to significantly contribute to the acoustic amenity of the area.

            Under the EPNR Regulation 14A, the assigned noise levels of Regulation 7 do not apply to waste collection
            (both domestic and commercial sources), provided certain conditions are met.

            To minimise amenity impact to the community, it is recommended that waste collection and loading to occur
            between the hours of 7am – 7pm Monday to Saturday.


            In summary, in view of the available information, we consider that the development will be able to comply with
            the EPNR. The predictions in this report consider that the assumptions and recommendations provided will be
            fulfilled and implemented.

                            Introduction
                            Overview
            Stantec has been appointed by CDC Data Centres Pty Ltd (c/o Developed Property) to undertake an acoustic
            assessment for the proposed new 145MW data centre facility at 582 Bickley Rd, Maddington WA 6109. The
            proposed development includes four (4) two storey data centre buildings.

            This Acoustic Report for Development Application:

                    Outlines the noise emissions associated with the project;

                    Establishes relevant acoustic criteria in accordance with current Legislation, Regulations, Council
                    Policies, Australian Standards and Design Guidelines;

                    Assesses noise emission from mechanical services and back-up generator associated to the
                    development, providing management measures or mitigation where required for compliance.

            Each acoustical aspect identified above has been addressed in this report with recommendations provided that
            aims to achieve a consistent acoustical outcome for the project. All advice provided in this report is for
            coordination with the project team and implementation by the respective disciplines.

            A glossary of acoustic terms used in this report is included in Appendix A.

            The recommendations made in this report are specific to the building design at the date of issue of this report. The building
            design is subject to change during the following design stages. Where this occurs, the assumptions made to inform the
            recommendations in the report may no longer be valid; therefore, further advice should be sought to ensure that the acoustic
            outcomes presented in this report are achieved.

            The performance of products referred to in this report are made to meet the acoustic requirements only. It does not consider
            other aspects including, but not limited to, thermal, wind, impact, structural, mechanical, national construction code, security
            and fire requirements. Relevant discipline reports, drawings and specifications should be referred to for conformance.

            This report relates to this specific project and must not be applied to any other project without prior consultation with Stantec.
            Designs and conditions can vary between projects causing significant variations in acoustic performance requirements and
            relevant subsequent advice to one project may not apply to another.

            This report shall not be relied upon as providing any warranties or guarantees of construction quality regarding acoustics.

                     Western Australian Environmental Protection (Noise) Regulation 1997 (EPNR);

                            Environmental Protection (Noise) Regulation 1997
            Environmental noise impacts resulting from the noise emissions from the project are addressed through the
            Environmental Protection Act 1986, with the regulatory requirements detailed in the Environmental Protection
            (Noise) Regulations 1997 (EPNR).

            The EPNR establishes the maximum permissible noise emission levels (assigned levels) to be received at all
            adjacent noise-sensitive premises during specific periods of the day as a result of the cumulative noise
            emissions from all sources proposed for the project site. Compliance to relevant noise limits outlined in the
            EPNR is compulsory.

            The EPNR states noise emissions from any premises are considered not to significantly contribute to the noise
            at a receiver if the noise emissions are 5 dB or more below the assigned levels.

            In brief, the assigned levels are determined by considering of the amount of commercial and industrial zones,
            as well as main transport corridors and sporting venues surrounding the noise sensitive premises. The assigned
            levels apply at premises receiving the noise (noise sensitive receiver) and not to areas within the project site or
            lot. In addition, the Environmental Protection (Noise) Regulations 1997 identify the following in Schedule 3,
            clause 2A:

               “If the land within either of the circles is categorised on the land use map as land in respect of which mixed
                  uses are permitted, the use of that land that results in the highest influencing factor is to be used in the
                                                     determination of the influencing factor.”

            surrounding the project location, these include the following at approximately 1km west of the project site:

                     Residential receivers along Kelvin Rd (e.g., 220 Kelvin Rd), Dale Pl (e.g., 102 Dale Pl) and Boyle Ln

                             Noise Character Adjustments
            Regulation 7 states that the noise character must be “free” of annoying characteristics, namely —
            •        Tonality, e.g. whining, droning;

            •        Modulation, e.g. like a siren; and

            •        Impulsiveness, e.g. banging, thumping.

            Regulation 9 (1) establishes the methodology for determining noise characteristics. If these characteristics
            cannot be reasonably and practicably removed, a series of adjustments to the measured levels are required,
            indicated in Table 5.

                      Regulation 14A
            The data centre requires continuous power supply to operate. It is proposed that operation of the Back-up
            Generators for continued power supply in the event of a major outage is considered Class 2 Works under the
            EPNR 14A. The generator operation may be considered activities associated with hazard or emergency
            management for the following reasons:
                    Power outages can lead to unsaved data being lost, interrupted processes or corrupted files. This can be
                    devastating in sectors such as finance, healthcare and cloud services;

                    Downtime disrupts data centre operations, potentially leading to contractual penalties, loss of customer
                    trust and missed business opportunities. Backup power ensures the site can continue running seamlessly
                    during grid outages;

                    Sudden power interruptions can damage sensitive hardware such as servers, cooling systems and
                    networking equipment. Backup systems help maintain stability, extending the lifespan of these assets;
                    and

                    Many industries require adherence to strict compliance standards regarding uptime, data protection and
                    disaster recovery. Backup power helps data centers meet their certifications and regulatory compliance.

            As an acoustic mitigation measure, all generators are proposed to be fitted with acoustic attenuation applied to
            intake, discharge and exhaust. Preliminary attenuation insertion loss values are provided in Appendix C.

                            Noise Modelling
            Noise modelling was undertaken in general accordance with DWER’s Guideline for the assessment of
            environmental noise emissions date May 2021.
            The assessment of each potential noise source against the EPNR criteria (LA10, LA1, or LAmax) is proportional to
            the period of the day, and the combined frequency and duration of each noise event. To assess a worst-case
            scenario, assessment has been conducted against the most stringent LA10 criteria.

                            Noise Propagation Algorithm
            Typical Meteorological Conditions
            The ISO 9613-2:1996 prediction algorithm has been used in this assessment. ISO 9613-2 specifies an
            engineering method for calculating the attenuation of sound during propagation outdoors in order to predict the
            levels of environmental noise at a distance from a variety of sources. The method predicts the equivalent
            continuous downwind octave band sound pressure level (as described in parts 1 to 3 of ISO 1996) under
            meteorological conditions favourable to propagation from sources of known sound emission.

            Worst-case Meteorological Conditions
            The CONCAWE algorithm has been selected to model worst-case meteorological conditions, as presented in
            Table 6. Conditions for enhancement of sound propagation have been considered (Draft Guideline:
            Environmental Noise for Prescribed Premises, WA Department of Environment Regulation 2016).

                            Air cooled chiller and PAC unit operational loading
            Air cooled chiller and PAC unit plant operating settings, and consequently noise emission, will vary depending
            on load requirements and environmental conditions. Cooling plant items are expected to operate at all hours in
            a capacity to support the load within the data halls. It is understood that chiller plant will operate at 100%
            capacity during typical operational conditions. During the night period capacity is understood to further reduce.
            PAC plant will similarly reduce in operating capacity to between 50-70% during the night period

            Equipment operating below 100% capacity can typically result in reductions in noise emission by 1-3dB (75%
            capacity to 50% capacity respectively). The following assumed reductions to the presented noise emission data
            in Table 7 are provided to account for variance in operating conditions (time periods as defined in the EPNR):

                      Day period: 0dB reduction (100% capacity, worst case);

                      Evening period: 1.5dB reduction (capacity reduced to 75%); and

                      Night period: 3dB reduction (capacity reduced to 50%).

                            Potential annoying characteristics of the sound
            An assessment has been conducted to evaluate potentially annoying characteristics of the sound of the
            proposed equipment, which if present require an adjustment (penalty) to the measured level at the receiver
            under the EPNR.

            Modulating and impulsive characteristics are not expected of the proposed equipment. Consideration has been
            given to potential tonal characteristics.

            Given that data from mechanical plant manufacturers is generally limited to broadband data or in 1/1 octave
            band value, it is not possible to objectively determine tonality, as it is described in the EPNR. 1/3 octave band
            data is required yet is typically unavailable. The assessment of these characteristics is carried out at the receiver
            location, approximately 300m from the site and across Tonkin Hwy for a typical residence.

            Analysis on the Chiller 1/1 octave band data of the source, interpolated to 1/3 octave band data, has been
            conducted based on the performance and operational characteristics. This shows that the anticipated tonal noise
            levels are not expected to present any significant concerns, with a maximum of 1.7dB difference between
            adjacent bands above 400Hz, and 3.5dB below 400Hz. It should be noted that this assessment is based on
            assumptions of the units and should be confirmed through measurements of the equipment once available. Any
            changes to the equipment characteristics will be required to be captured in an updated acoustic assessment.

            A similar study has been conducted on the Generator and predicted generator flue noise. Similar to the above,
            analysis was conducted on the 1/1 octave band data of the source, interpolated to 1/3 octave band data, based
            on information provided by the manufacturer. This shows a maximum of 1.5 dB difference between the adjacent
            bands above 400Hz, and 2.4 dB below 400Hz for the predicted regen noise from the flues. A maximum
            difference of 4.6dB between the adjacent bands above 400Hz, and 5.8dB below 400Hz for the generator itself.
            Only 1 generator is expected to operate in typical testing scenarios and the receiver contributions are
            significantly below that of the Chillers.

            The PAC units are not expected to be significant contributors to received noise levels and therefore tonal
            characteristics are not expected at the receiving locations.

                            Shielding provided by building massing
            The massing of buildings has been modelled as:

                    Generator plant – it is noted the generators are stacked and some shielding to intake or discharge side is
                    provided by the data centre buildings, however the generator exhaust has no shielding;

                    Chiller plant and PAC – services and plant rooms are modelled as solid, however the majority of rooftop
                    units have no shielding offered. Plant decks are modelled as acoustically “open” (e.g. grid mesh), with no
                    solid acoustic screening.

            The location of plant is as per the Development Application site plans, noting multiple redundancy for rooftop
            chillers (many units do not run in typical operation, only as back-ups). The results of the assessment are sensitive
            to plant location and will have up to 4 dB variance based on the positions of specific operational equipment.

            As such, during the most sensitive periods; Sundays, Evenings and Night-times (as defined in the EPNR), the
            selection of Chiller units operating will need to be managed such that the operational units are positioned
            towards the middle of the buildings, away from sensitive receivers

                    Limiting the generator maintenance and testing for day period only (Monday to Friday 0900 – 1600);

                            Discussion
            Based on the above predicted results, during typical operations a marginal exceedance of +1dB is noted at the
            receivers under worst-case meteorological conditions (CONCAWE algorithm).
            However, compliance is expected under typical meteorological conditions (ISO algorithm) at the receivers
            during all operational periods. The difference of 1 dB is typically not perceptible.
            Emergency operations (during a power outage) are expected to exceed the assigned levels of the EPNR at
            night-time, however would only be marginal +1 dB in the evening and would maintain compliance with the EPNR
            during the day (Monday – Saturday).

                            Loading Dock
            Based on the latest architectural drawings, loading dock is proposed to be located on ground level adjacent to
            the data centre buildings MA.3 and MA.4 and common loading dock shared by buildings MA.1 and MA.2 as
            shown in Figure 7.




            Figure 7: Proposed Loading Dock Locations
            It is noted that vehicles of various sizes up to 19m semi-articulated trucks will be servicing the proposed
            development. Based on the existing adjacent uses (truck and industrial vehicle storage yards), the noise
            emission from trucks accessing the site is not expected to significantly contribute to the acoustic amenity of the
            area.

                            Waste Collection
            Based on the drawings, it is assumed that the waste collection activities will be conducted adjacent to the car
            park area of the data centre buildings. It is recommended that these activities occur between 0700 to 1900 hours
            on Monday to Saturday.

            Under the EPNR Regulation 14A, the assigned noise levels of Regulation 7 do not apply to waste collection
            (both domestic and commercial sources).

              LAeqT                         The constant A-weighted sound which has the same energy as the fluctuating

                                            sound level meter with a microphone.
              Sound Power Level:            Ten times the logarithm to the base 10 of the ratio of the sound power of the
                                            source to the reference sound power.

                 ASSESSMENT
                 Preface
                 The applicant proposes construction of an office (large) at 582 Bickley Road, Maddington (Location Plate 1).
                 The site is within a declared bushfire prone area and located within the administrative area of the City of
                 Gosnells (Map of Bushfire Prone Area Plate 2). The site is zoned for Business Development in the City’s Local
                 Planning Scheme 6. There are no plans to change the extent of the classified vegetation/extent of the Bushfire
                 Prone Area, that may be associated with plans for revegetation of areas within 100 m of the site.
                 The proposed office is development that is required to be assessed for its compliance with the siting
                 requirements in State Planning Policy 3.7 Planning in Bushfire Prone Areas (‘SPP 3.7’) and the bushfire
                 protection criterial described in the Guidelines v1.4, but only to the extent that is within the Bushfire Prone
                 Area.
                 The proposed building is a class 7b building. It is not a class of building subject to the bushfire construction
                 standard (Construction in Bushfire Prone Areas) described at Part G5 Volume 2 National Construction Code
                 2019 (and unchanged in NCC 2022).
                 1.   Proposal details
                 The site is approximately 7.8 ha and historically cleared of trees. The site is located in a triangular area
                 between Tonkin Highway, Kelvin Road and Bickley Road. Kenwick Road leads from Kelvin Road and is central
                 within the triangle.
                 The site is flat, and vacant.
                 The proposal is a large data centre (Site Plan Plate 3). It comprises 3 large separate 2 story buildings and 1
                 single story building each with a front of house (office) and power generator banks. The proposal also includes
                 a gate house at the access from Kenwick Road, and a power substation at the east of the site.
                 The site is within an established industrial area and has access to a reticulated water supply.
                 2.   Environmental considerations
                 No clearing of regulated vegetation is proposed.
                 Future landscaping is largely outside the Bushfire Prone Area map but is proposed to be provided as low threat
                 in compliance with AS3959:2018 s.2.2.3.2(f).
                 3.   Bushfire assessment results
                 A Bushfire Attack Level assessment following Method 1 AS 3959:2018, and the DPLH Visual guide for bushfire
                 risk assessment in Western Australia, and using an FFDI of 80, has been undertaken.
                 No habitable building exceeds BAL 29.
                 4.   Identification of bushfire hazard issues
                 The site is adjoined by lots awaiting development for commercial purpose (grassland) and the Tonkin Highway
                 road reserve.
                 The habitable buildings are outside of direct flame contact, but the site is within range to be affected by ember
                 attack from a fire in the Perth Hills/Darling Scarp. Katabatic winds could drive embers (from the east) affecting
                 a broad area at the foothills, including the site.
                 The likelihood of a bushfire is considered low, and vigilance to avoid the storage and location of flammable
                 materials near buildings is a recommended risk treatment.
                 The consequence of a bushfire is considered minor. It is not expected that the building operation would be
                 disrupted beyond the immediate bushfire event.




                 ENVISION BUSHFIRE PROTECTION     BUSSELTON l PERTH
